newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale prices rise on energy-cost spike.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale prices rise on energy-cost spike.

text.p: A sharp jump in energy costs pushed wholesale prices up more strongly than anticipated in November, the government said Wednesday, though not enough to change the outlook for tame inflation overall.
The Labour Department said its Producer Price Index, which measures price changes at the wholesale level, rose 0.4 percent in November, after rising at the same rate in October.
Excluding volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core rate rose just 0.1 percent last month after falling 0.3 percent in October.
"There is no inflation out there except for food and energy," said economist David Wyss of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass., "And the big energy price increase I believe is temporary."
During November, energy prices jumped 2.3 percent -- the biggest gain since a 2.7 percent rise in April, the department said. Energy prices rose 1.9 percent in October.
But food prices fell 0.1 percent after a 0.8 percent rise in October. It was the first drop since a 0.5 percent decline in April, suggesting the worst was over for food costs.

Analysts said the report pointed to tame inflation and virtually assured that the Federal Reserve would hold interest rates steady when the central bank's policy-makers hold their last meeting of the year on Tuesday.

"The overall outlook is that producer price inflation is well-behaved and any pressure that is out there is narrowly confined to the energy sector," said Raphael Marrone, an economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell of New York.
Some analysts said energy prices would fall next year.

"With Iraqi oil now flowing it appears that energy prices will move lower by the end of the winter heating season and that by this time next year oil prices will be below current levels," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla.

Iraq started pumping oil on Tuesday under an agreement with the United Nations for it to resume limited oil sales for the first time since invading neighbouring Kuwait in 1990. Iraq is to use the proceeds to buy food.
"The bottom line is that the trend of inflation at the wholesale goods level is still benign," Reaser said, adding that should be "soothing news" for policy-makers at the Fed.

While prices for merchandise appear tame at the wholesale and retail level, some analysts said rising wages could become a concern for Fed policy-makers, though few expected a rate increase at next week's meeting.

Gasoline prices rose 2.8 percent in November while heating oil prices fell 0.4 percent. Prices for natural gas jumped 3.8 percent, a record, beating the 3.4 percent gain recorded in December 1995, the department said.
Prices for new cars rose a sharp 0.5 percent in November after falling 1.6 percent in October. Tobacco prices fell 0.1 percent last month, after rising 0.3 percent in October.
Analysts saw little sign of threatening "pipeline pressures" arising from sharp jumps in raw materials or goods for further processing that might later be reflected in higher retail prices.
Prices of intermediate goods rose 0.2 percent in November after being unchanged in October. Prices of crude goods rose 1.8 percent after a 0.6 percent decline in October.
